Minimum Requirements for Verification (~1 minute)
Your machine must meet all of the following to be eligible for verification.
Component
Minimum Requirement
OS
Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS minimum, 24.04 LTS recommended. Server edition only; releases above 24.04 are not supported
GPU
NVIDIA Maxwell or newer, all GPUs the same model. More than 7 GB VRAM per GPU
NVIDIA Driver
Must support CUDA 11.8 or newer. Latest stable recommended
CUDA
11.8 or newer. On ARM64, 12.6 or newer. Latest recommended
CPU
x86_64 or ARM64 with AVX support. 2 physical cores per GPU
RAM
At least 95% of total GPU VRAM (0.95 × VRAM per GPU × number of GPUs)
Storage
SSD. At least a 200 GB dedicated partition for Docker storage, and 20 GB free on the root partition
PCIe
More than 2.85 GiB/s per GPU
Network
500 Mbps download and upload. Wired Ethernet, fiber recommended
Ports
Public IPv4 address with 5 forwarded ports per GPU (100 recommended). CGNAT and shared ISP IPs are not supported
SSH Access
SSH key authentication only. Password login enabled will fail verification
Updates
Update the kernel and all packages before running the installer
For the full list and the latest updates, see Minimum Requirements for Verification.

6.  Hairpinning Behavior

   If two hosts (called X1 and X2) are behind the same NAT and
   exchanging traffic, the NAT may allocate an address on the outside of
   the NAT for X2, called X2':x2'.  If X1 sends traffic to X2':x2', it
   goes to the NAT, which must relay the traffic from X1 to X2.  This is
   referred to as hairpinning and is illustrated below.







Audet & Jennings         Best Current Practice                 [Page 16]
 
RFC 4787              NAT UDP Unicast Requirements          January 2007


     NAT
   +----+ from X1:x1 to X2':x2'   +-----+ X1':x1'
   | X1 |>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>--+---
   +----+                         |  v  |
                                  |  v  |
                                  |  v  |
                                  |  v  |
   +----+ from X1':x1' to X2:x2   |  v  | X2':x2'
   | X2 |<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<<--+---
   +----+                         +-----+

                           Hairpinning Behavior

   Hairpinning allows two endpoints on the internal side of the NAT to
   communicate even if they only use each other's external IP addresses
   and ports.

   More formally, a NAT that supports hairpinning forwards packets
   originating from an internal address, X1:x1, destined for an external
   address X2':x2' that has an active mapping to an internal address
   X2:x2, back to that internal address, X2:x2.  Note that typically X1'
   is the same as X2'.

   Furthermore, the NAT may present the hairpinned packet with either an
   internal (X1:x1) or an external (X1':x1') source IP address and port.
   Therefore, the hairpinning NAT behavior can be either "External
   source IP address and port" or "Internal source IP address and port".
   "Internal source IP address and port" may cause problems by confusing
   implementations that expect an external IP address and port.

      a) A NAT Hairpinning behavior MUST be "External source IP address
         and port".

   Justification:  This requirement is to allow communications between
      two endpoints behind the same NAT when they are trying each
      other's external IP addresses.

      a) Using the external source IP address is necessary for

    try:
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        device_properties = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(device)

## Fresh Install Self-Test

The installer can start self-test automatically after the daemon comes online. On a fresh host, it may wait about 10 minutes before listing the machine and starting the temporary diagnostic instance.

On the host, watch only for the planned self-test window; press `Ctrl+C` when the self-test ends and confirm that `tail` exits:

#!/bin/bash
#INFO: Redirect all output to self_test.log
exec &>>/var/lib/vastai_kaalia/self_test.log

MACHINE_ID=$1
GPU_PPH=$2
MIN_COUNT=$3
RESERVED_DISCOUNT=$4
SERVER_URL=$5
MACHINE_API_KEY=$6
SESSION_API_KEY=$7

export VAST_URL=$SERVER_URL

echo "========================================="
echo "Starting self-test for machine $MACHINE_ID"
echo "Server: $SERVER_URL"
echo "Timestamp: $(date)"
echo "========================================="

echo "Waiting 10 minutes for daemon to initialize..."
sleep 10m
echo "Done waiting."

echo "Checking if machine $MACHINE_ID is already listed..."
if python3 /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/vast show machine $MACHINE_ID --raw --url $SERVER_URL --api-key $SESSION_API_KEY 2>&1 | grep -q '"listed": true'; then
  echo "Machine $MACHINE_ID is already listed. Exiting early."
  echo "Timestamp: $(date)"
  echo "========================================="
  exit 0
fi

## How Verification Works

Verification is automated. A machine becomes eligible when it passes self-test and meets reliability, performance, hardware, network, and marketplace gates.

<Note>

Verification
When your machine is added to the platform, it will have the Unverified status. This just means that it has not yet had time to build up its reliability score and demonstrate that it can reliably sustain instances and stay connected to the platform. While it has this status, it is still searchable, but will not show up on the default search filters.
Machine verification is fully automated, and runs at least once each day. The system evaluates each machine using multiple criteria, including GPU model, demand, uptime, network stability, DLPerf, and overall reliability. There's no fixed timeline for verification. The best way to improve your chances is to ensure your machine passes all system tests, maintains high uptime, stable network connectivity, and strong DLPerf performance, and that it operates reliably over time.
Support is unable to expedite or manually influence this process. You can read more about how verification works here.

Minimum Requirements for Verification (~1 minute)
Your machine must meet all of the following to be eligible for verification.
Component
Minimum Requirement
OS
Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS minimum, 24.04 LTS recommended. Server edition only; releases above 24.04 are not supported
GPU
NVIDIA Maxwell or newer, all GPUs the same model. More than 7 GB VRAM per GPU
NVIDIA Driver
Must support CUDA 11.8 or newer. Latest stable recommended
CUDA
11.8 or newer. On ARM64, 12.6 or newer. Latest recommended
CPU
x86_64 or ARM64 with AVX support. 2 physical cores per GPU
RAM

Network Setup (~15 mins)
Port Requirements
- At least 5 open ports per GPU (100 open ports per GPU is recommended).
- The port range must be continuous, for both TCP and UDP, such as 16384-32768.
- The Vast software installer will prompt you for an open port range, so be prepared.
You can change the port range later by writing it to /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_port_range:
sudo bash -c 'echo -n "<START_PORT>-<END_PORT>" > /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_port_range'
Make sure there is no trailing newline.
You can still list a machine without open ports, but it is unlikely to get rentals and will not qualify for verification.
IP Requirements
- A dynamic IP is acceptable, but a static IP is preferred. The IP must be a public IPv4 address — CGNAT and shared ISP IPs are not supported.
- By default, your machine's public IP is the incoming IP that connects to our server.
For most networks this is sufficient, but sysadmins of unusual datacenter networks may want to override this behavior (useful for some asymmetric NATs/firewalls) by writing the IP to /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_ipaddr:

### I fear I will decrease my reliability from restarting my machine and potentially lose my verification.

A drop in reliability does not by itself cost you your verification. What does is an active error. A machine stays de-verified while it has one, and is verified again once the error clears.

Restarting during an active rental does cost you reliability. Schedule a maintenance window first to keep the penalty smaller and recover sooner.

**Recovery:**
Fix the issue and restore stability; the system will **automatically** transition back to Verified once system confirms healthy operation.
This process may take some time, as the system ensures that the issue is fully resolved before restoring verification. Most error messages are cleared within 1-2 hours of resolution.

import torch
import os
import sys
import psutil

SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_MIB = 2_000_000
SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_BYTES = SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_MIB * 1024 * 1024


def required_system_ram_bytes(total_vram):
    return min(int(0.95 * total_vram), SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_BYTES)


def main():
    # Number of GPUs
    NUM_GPUS = torch.cuda.device_count()

    # VRAM of GPUs
    total_vram = sum([torch.cuda.get_device_properties(i).total_memory for i in range(NUM_GPUS)])

    # Check that at least 98% of VRAM is free on each GPU
    for i in range(NUM_GPUS):
        vram = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(i).total_memory
        vram_used = torch.cuda.memory_allocated(i) + torch.cuda.memory_reserved(i)
        if vram_used > 0.02 * vram:
            print(f'Less than 98% of VRAM is free on GPU {i}.')
            return 1

    # System total memory (RAM)
    total_ram = psutil.virtual_memory().total

    # Number of CPU cores
    num_cpu_cores = psutil.cpu_count(logical=False)

    required_ram = required_system_ram_bytes(total_vram)
    if total_ram < required_ram:
        print(
            'System total memory is less than the required minimum '
            f'({required_ram} bytes, capped at {SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_MIB} MiB).'
        )
        return 1

    if num_cpu_cores < 2 * NUM_GPUS:
        print('There are less than 2 CPU cores per GPU.')
        return 1

    print('System meets the minimum requirements.')
    return 0

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())

import torch
import os
import sys
import psutil

SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_MIB = 2_000_000
SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_BYTES = SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_MIB * 1024 * 1024


def required_system_ram_bytes(total_vram):
    return min(int(0.95 * total_vram), SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_BYTES)


def main():
    # Number of GPUs
    NUM_GPUS = torch.cuda.device_count()

    # VRAM of GPUs
    total_vram = sum([torch.cuda.get_device_properties(i).total_memory for i in range(NUM_GPUS)])

    # Check that at least 98% of VRAM is free on each GPU
    for i in range(NUM_GPUS):
        vram = torch.cuda.get_device_properties(i).total_memory
        vram_used = torch.cuda.memory_allocated(i) + torch.cuda.memory_reserved(i)
        if vram_used > 0.02 * vram:
            print(f'Less than 98% of VRAM is free on GPU {i}.')
            return 1

    # System total memory (RAM)
    total_ram = psutil.virtual_memory().total

    # Number of CPU cores
    num_cpu_cores = psutil.cpu_count(logical=False)

    required_ram = required_system_ram_bytes(total_vram)
    if total_ram < required_ram:
        print(
            'System total memory is less than the required minimum '
            f'({required_ram} bytes, capped at {SYSTEM_RAM_REQUIREMENT_CAP_MIB} MiB).'
        )
        return 1

    if num_cpu_cores < 2 * NUM_GPUS:
        print('There are less than 2 CPU cores per GPU.')
        return 1

    print('System meets the minimum requirements.')
    return 0

if __name__ == '__main__':
    sys.exit(main())

Network Setup (~15 mins)
Port Requirements
- At least 5 open ports per GPU (100 open ports per GPU is recommended).
- The port range must be continuous, for both TCP and UDP, such as 16384-32768.

sudo bash -c 'echo -n "<START_PORT>-<END_PORT>" > /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_port_range'
Make sure there is no trailing newline.
You can still list a machine without open ports, but it is unlikely to get rentals and will not qualify for verification.

- A dynamic IP is acceptable, but a static IP is preferred. The IP must be a public IPv4 address — CGNAT and shared ISP IPs are not supported.
- By default, your machine's public IP is the incoming IP that connects to our server.
For most networks this is sufficient, but sysadmins of unusual datacenter networks may want to override this behavior (useful for some asymmetric NATs/firewalls) by writing the IP to /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_ipaddr:
sudo bash -c 'echo -n "<YOUR_IP_ADDRESS>" > /var/lib/vastai_kaalia/host_ipaddr'

- Minimum: 10 Mbps upload/download per machine, but rentals are very unlikely at this speed.

def search_offers(client: VastClient, query: dict = None, offer_type: str = "on-demand",
                  order: list = None, limit: int = None, storage: float = 5.0,
                  no_default: bool = False, disable_bundling: bool = False) -> list:
    """Search for instance offers using a query dict.

    Args:
        client: VastClient instance.
        query: Pre-parsed query dict of filters (e.g. {"gpu_name": {"eq": "RTX 3090"}}).
        offer_type: One of "on-demand", "reserved", or "bid".
        order: List of [field, direction] pairs, e.g. [["score", "desc"]].
        limit: Max number of results.
        storage: Allocated storage in GiB for pricing (default 5.0).
        no_default: If True, skip default filters.
        disable_bundling: Deprecated bundling flag.

    Returns:
        List of offer dicts.
    """
    if no_default:
        q = query or {}
    else:
        q = {"verified": {"eq": True}, "external": {"eq": False},
             "rentable": {"eq": True}, "rented": {"eq": False}}
        if query:
            q.update(query)

    if order is not None:
        q["order"] = order
    else:
        q["order"] = [["score", "desc"]]

    q["type"] = offer_type
    if offer_type == "interruptible":
        q["type"] = "bid"

    if limit:
        q["limit"] = int(limit)
    q["allocated_storage"] = storage

    if disable_bundling:
        q["disable_bundling"] = True

    r = client.post("/bundles/", json_data=q)
    r.raise_for_status()

## Comparing your ranking

There are over 10,000+ listings on Vast, and search only displays a small subset. You will usually not be able to find any one specific machine through most normal searches. This is expected and intentional behavior of our system. You can use `vastai search offers 'machine_id=MACHINE_ID verified=any'`, to see your machine's listing.
